lines.text: DWF1 - Operational databases vs analytical systems
The database that records an order correctly is solving a different job from the system that analyzes eighteen months of orders. Running
heavy analytical joins on operational systems can hurt the business and still fail to preserve historical meaning.
Classify systems by workload instead of product name; separate transaction integrity from analytical history; explain why analytical copies need
Course 1 database basics and C2-02/C2-03 grain concepts. No engineering platform experience required.
5. New words before we use them
Operational system: System primarily designed to record/run day-to-day business transactions. Analytical system: System designed for historical scans,
aggregations, cross-source analysis and governed reporting. Workload isolation: Keeping heavy analytics from competing directly with critical transaction
VISUAL/SOURCE ROUTE: Microsoft Fabric warehouse module: Understand data warehouses (7 min) is recommended visual context.
After watching/opening: return to this lesson and reproduce the worked example from your own file/query/report. Save course-task evidence, not a screenshot of the
Cash register vs boardroom mirror: an operational system records the latest business transaction quickly; an analytical system reorganizes
accumulated history so many rows can be scanned, grouped and compared without disrupting the operational workflow.
Teacher demonstration - do this once with me, then close the example before your fresh task.
Operational question: Did order O1023 post, reserve inventory and record payment correctly? This needs current transactional correctness.
Analytical question: Which customer segments drove revenue growth by region over 18 months? This needs history, broad scans and stable
If Customer.Region changes today, the operational system may simply store the current region. Historical reporting may need the region that
was valid when each sale occurred.
Sketch Source OLTP -> governed analytical copy -> semantic/report layer. Note that the copied data is now subject to freshness and lineage
Write one reason not to run a large executive-history query directly against the production order database.
8. What you should see / be able to say
You can classify a workload as operational or analytical and name the history/freshness controls that appear after data is copied.
The distinction comes from the job the system performs, not from calling one database 'modern' and another 'old'. Professional upgrade: Architectures often
include operational sources plus analytical stores, replicas or lake/warehouse layers. The right boundary protects transaction systems while giving analysts
1. Calling any SQL database OLTP and any warehouse OLAP. | 2. Assuming operational current-state rows preserve historical attribution. | 3.
Ignoring source-system load/availability when analysts query production. | 4. Treating copied data as automatically current/trusted.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Write the user action first: record a transaction or analyze many historical records? Then ask latency, concurrency, history and scan pattern. Save the
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: an insurance claims app and an executive loss-analysis platform. Classify five example queries/actions and justify placement.
For each case record workload type, history need, latency and one risk if run in the wrong system.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain operational versus analytical systems using 'run the business' versus 'understand the business' without saying one is better.
Save classification first. Changed retry uses hospital appointment booking versus care-capacity analytics.
Workload table + architecture sketch + risk/freshness controls + explain-back. After saving evidence, continue to DWF2.
OLTP and OLAP are workload patterns, not insults about schema quality. A normalized transactional schema can be excellent for updates
Compare OLTP and OLAP on transaction size, concurrency, update patterns, history, query shapes and common schema design; recognize
that analytical systems can still be near-real-time.
DWF1 workload separation and basic relational database concepts.
5. New words before we use them
OLTP: Online Transaction Processing: many small operational reads/writes with transactional integrity. OLAP: Online Analytical Processing: analytical
scans/aggregations over larger/historical datasets. Normalization: Structuring relational data to reduce redundancy and protect update integrity.
VISUAL/SOURCE ROUTE: Book-led; Microsoft warehouse module reinforces warehouse workload purpose.
After watching/opening: return to this lesson and reproduce the worked example from your own file/query/report. Save course-task evidence, not a screenshot of the
Checkout lane vs warehouse scan: OLTP optimizes many small concurrent reads/writes around current transactions; OLAP optimizes broad
analytical scans, joins and aggregations over larger historical sets. Workload shape drives architecture.
Teacher demonstration - do this once with me, then close the example before your fresh task.
OLTP: 'Did customer C12's payment complete?' likely touches a few rows and needs fast, correct transaction handling.
OLAP: 'Which segments/regions drove margin change by quarter?' scans/aggregates many records and may join historical dimensions.
Explain why normalized Customer, Order, OrderLine, Payment tables can be right for transactions.
Explain why an analytical dimensional model may denormalize descriptive attributes around facts for simpler reporting.
Record that OLAP does not require stale data: near-real-time analytical copies can exist if the business needs that latency.
8. What you should see / be able to say
A workload comparison based on actual behavior, with no claim that normalization is bad design.
The same business can need both structures because transaction writes and analytical scans optimize different outcomes. Professional upgrade: Hybrid and
near-real-time patterns blur strict boundaries, but the workload questions remain useful: transaction integrity, scan volume, freshness, governance and cost.
1. OLAP = old data only. | 2. Denormalized = automatically faster/correct. | 3. OLTP schema is 'wrong' because BI queries are verbose. | 4.
Choosing architecture before defining query/latency/concurrency needs.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
For each workload write: writes per second, rows touched, history span, common query shape, acceptable latency and consistency need. Save the
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: food-delivery order placement, courier tracking, daily finance close and monthly cohort analysis. Classify OLTP/OLAP/near-real-time
Each classification cites workload properties, not a vendor/product label.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain why the same company normally has both OLTP and OLAP workloads.
Attempt first. Changed retry classifies banking transfers and regulatory analytics.
OLTP/OLAP matrix + workload reasoning + explain-back. After saving evidence, continue to DWF3.
A warehouse is not just a large database. It is a governed analytical system that integrates sources, preserves useful history and serves
Describe warehouse purpose, subject areas, load/ownership responsibilities, historical behavior, dimensional serving and current Fabric
5. New words before we use them
Data warehouse: Governed analytical store integrating business data for historical analysis/reporting. Subject area: Business domain organized for analysis,
such as Sales, Finance or Customer Service. Data mart: Curated analytical subset focused on a business area/audience.
VISUAL/SOURCE ROUTE: Microsoft Learn - Get started with data warehouses in Fabric (1h16m). Required: Understand data warehouses 7m + warehouses in
After watching/opening: return to this lesson and reproduce the worked example from your own file/query/report. Save course-task evidence, not a screenshot of the
Historical library: source systems send changing operational records into a durable analytical store where integration, history and business-ready
structures are kept long enough for repeatable cross-period questions.
Teacher demonstration - do this once with me, then close the example before your fresh task.
Sources: order system, CRM/customer master and targets. List owners and expected arrival/freshness.
Landing/staging captures source data and validates schema/types before business modeling.
Warehouse/core contains conformed DimCustomer, DimProduct, DimDate plus FactSales and FactTarget at declared grains.
Semantic/report layer uses those governed structures instead of rejoining raw exports monthly.
Define ownership for definitions, loads, quality, retention and failure response. A warehouse without operations/ownership is incomplete.
8. What you should see / be able to say
A warehouse architecture tied to business processes, history and ownership rather than a copy of every source table.
The design creates a controlled analytical contract between changing operational sources and stable reporting. Professional upgrade: Fabric Warehouse is a
current SaaS relational warehouse on OneLake/Delta with T-SQL and enterprise BI use cases, but durable warehouse design does not depend on Fabric.
1. Copy every source table and call it a warehouse. | 2. Start with tables before business processes/consumers. | 3. No owner for failed refresh
or KPI definition. | 4. Assume today's dimension value should rewrite yesterday's facts.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Start with business questions/processes, then facts/grains, dimensions/history, sources/loads, quality and consumers. Save the genuine attempt before
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: design a high-level warehouse for Sales + Support + Targets without choosing a cloud vendor.
Every proposed table/layer has a purpose, grain/role, upstream source and downstream consumer.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain the difference between 'a database containing lots of data' and a governed warehouse.
Attempt first. Changed retry uses healthcare operations.
Architecture + subject/process map + ownership/freshness notes + explain-back. After saving evidence, continue to DWF4.
DWF4 - Facts, dimensions and dimensional modeling
Mixing Sales, Tickets and Targets because they share Customer or Region produces grain errors. Dimensional modeling starts with the
measurable business process and one-row meaning.
Declare fact grain first; choose fact measures/foreign keys; design dimensions/conformed dimensions; keep different processes/grains
C2-03 modeling helps, but warehouse-side dimensional modeling is taught again from first principles.
5. New words before we use them
Fact: Table storing measurable business events/snapshots at explicit grain. Dimension: Descriptive entity/context used to filter, group and label facts.
Conformed dimension: Consistently defined dimension reused across multiple facts.
VISUAL/SOURCE ROUTE: Microsoft Fabric dimensional modeling overview + optional star-schema visual from C2-03.
After watching/opening: return to this lesson and reproduce the worked example from your own file/query/report. Save course-task evidence, not a screenshot of the
Receipt plus labels: each fact row records one declared business event at one grain; conformed dimensions provide reusable descriptive context. A
target or second process stays a separate fact when its grain/process differs.
Teacher demonstration - do this once with me, then close the example before your fresh task.
FactSales grain = one row per order line. Measures may include Quantity, GrossSales, Discount, NetSales.
FactReturns grain = one row per return event/item. Keep it separate from sales if the process/grain differs.
FactTarget grain = one row per Region-Month. Do not join target value directly to every order line.
Conformed DimDate/DimProduct/DimCustomer/DimRegion can filter compatible facts consistently.
Validate each fact's business key uniqueness expectations and show which dimensions apply at its grain.
8. What you should see / be able to say
A star-schema design where every fact has a written grain and higher-grain facts do not multiply through transaction rows.
Processes remain separate while shared dimensions provide consistent analysis. Professional upgrade: Fabric's dimensional-model guidance recommends
star schemas for warehouse analytics, but grain/conformed-dimension principles transfer to any warehouse platform.
1. Choose columns before declaring grain. | 2. One giant fact for unrelated processes. | 3. Treat target table as a dimension. | 4. Fact-to-fact joins
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Write 'one row in this fact means...' for every measurable table. Separate facts whenever that sentence differs materially. Save the genuine attempt
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: parcel Shipments, ShipmentEvents and HubMonthlyTargets with Customer/Hub/Date dimensions.
Trace five analytical questions to a fact at the right grain; prove target cannot duplicate through shipment rows.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain why two tables that both contain CustomerID still may belong to separate facts.
Attempt first. Changed retry uses clinic encounters, billing and staffing targets.
Fact-grain register + star sketch + conformed-dimension map + validation + explain-back. After saving evidence, continue to DWF5.
DWF5 - Surrogate keys and business keys
If a source business key is the only warehouse key, historical versions of the same customer/product cannot be represented cleanly. If you
invent surrogate keys without preserving the business key, lineage disappears.
Distinguish source/domain business keys from warehouse-generated surrogate keys; use surrogate keys to identify dimension
records/versions while preserving business keys for lineage/change detection.
DWF4 dimensions/facts and basic primary/foreign-key concepts.
5. New words before we use them
Business key: Identifier from the source/business domain for a real entity. Surrogate key: Warehouse-generated key identifying a dimension record/version.
Foreign key: Key stored on a fact to reference the appropriate dimension row/version.
VISUAL/SOURCE ROUTE: Book-led; DWF6 visual makes the key/history relationship concrete.
After watching/opening: return to this lesson and reproduce the worked example from your own file/query/report. Save course-task evidence, not a screenshot of the
Passport vs warehouse key: the business key identifies the source entity, while a warehouse surrogate key identifies one warehouse dimension
row/version. Facts reference the stable surrogate so source key changes/history do not rewrite old facts.
Teacher demonstration - do this once with me, then close the example before your fresh task.
Business key CustomerID = C005 remains the identity of the same real customer.
Warehouse row 101 may represent C005 / West / old effective period.
Warehouse row 155 may represent C005 / South / current period. CustomerKey differs because the dimension version differs.
FactSales stores the surrogate CustomerKey appropriate to the sale's historical attribution, while CustomerID remains in dimension for
Validate no two dimension rows share a surrogate key and each business key's historical rows obey the intended current/effective-date rules.
8. What you should see / be able to say
A clear key strategy explaining real-world identity versus warehouse-record identity.
The warehouse can keep multiple versions without pretending the customer itself has multiple source identities. Professional upgrade: Surrogate keys are
especially useful for SCD2 and multi-source conformance. Business keys may require source-system namespace or matching logic in real warehouses.
1. Surrogate key replaces/erases business key. | 2. Hash/random key chosen without governance just because it sounds advanced. | 3. Facts
link to current dimension version regardless of event date. | 4. Business key assumed unique across multiple sources without source/system
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Ask: Which key did the source/business give us? Which key must uniquely identify a warehouse row/version? Keep both roles explicit. Save the
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: Employee E104 changes department twice. Design DimEmployee key columns and fact linkage for historical labor cost.
Surrogate uniqueness, business-key preservation and fact-to-correct-version logic are testable.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain business key versus surrogate key without saying 'natural keys are bad'.
Attempt first. Changed retry uses Product SKU reused across source systems.
Key register + sample history rows + fact foreign-key mapping + explain-back. After saving evidence, continue to DWF6.
If a customer moves from West to South and you overwrite Region, last year's sales can suddenly appear under today's region. SCD rules
decide whether dimension changes rewrite history or preserve it.
Choose SCD behavior by attribute/business need; contrast Type 1 overwrite and Type 2 versioning; design SCD2 effective dates/current
DWF5 business/surrogate keys and DWF4 fact grain.
5. New words before we use them
SCD: Slowly Changing Dimension: pattern for handling changes to descriptive dimension attributes. Type 1: Overwrite current value; prior value not
preserved in that dimension history. Type 2: Insert a new dimension version and expire the old version to preserve historical attribution.
VISUAL/SOURCE ROUTE: Recommended: Microsoft Fabric SCD Type 2 tutorial/article visuals; optional external SCD walkthrough only if it clarifies version
After watching/opening: return to this lesson and reproduce the worked example from your own file/query/report. Save course-task evidence, not a screenshot of the
Timeline cards: Type 1 replaces the label on the current card; Type 2 closes the old card and opens a new dated version. A fact chooses the
dimension version whose effective interval contains the event date.
Teacher demonstration - do this once with me, then close the example before your fresh task.
Current row: CustomerKey 101, CustomerID C005, Region West, EffectiveFrom 2025-01-01, EffectiveTo open-ended, IsCurrent true.
Source says Region South effective 2026-04-15. Decide Region needs Type 2 history; perhaps spelling correction of CustomerName could be
Expire old row at the agreed boundary and set IsCurrent false.
Insert new surrogate-key row for C005/South effective at change time with IsCurrent true.
For a sale on 2026-03-01 use old version; for 2026-05-01 use new version. Validate no overlapping effective ranges and exactly one current
8. What you should see / be able to say
A dimension history table that preserves the approved historical meaning without overlapping versions.
The business key stays C005 while surrogate keys distinguish versions. Professional upgrade: Current Fabric Data Factory documentation includes concrete
Type 1 and Type 2 implementation patterns, but this lesson assesses vendor-neutral history design rather than copying one tool flow.
1. Type 2 every attribute automatically. | 2. Two current rows for one business key. | 3. Effective ranges overlap by a day/instant. | 4. Fact load
joins only on business key and always receives current surrogate key.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Write the historical reporting question for each changed attribute. If prior state matters, design versioning; then draw effective-time intervals before
coding. Save the genuine attempt before review.
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: Agent Team and JobTitle change on different dates; decide Type 1/2 per attribute and build valid SCD2 history.
One current row per business key; no overlaps; each event date resolves to exactly one intended dimension version.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain how Type 2 prevents today's customer region from rewriting yesterday's revenue.
Attempt first. Changed retry uses Product Category history.
Attribute SCD policy + history rows + overlap/current tests + event-to-version mapping + explain-back. After saving evidence, continue to DWF7.
People use ETL and ELT as labels for entire architectures even when they have not defined where transformation actually occurs. The
durable question is where each validation/transformation runs and what raw history is retained.
Contrast transform-before-target ETL with load-before-transform ELT; document landing, execution location, compute/governance/security
DWF3 warehouse architecture and PYA/C2-01 transformation concepts.
5. New words before we use them
ETL: Extract, Transform, Load: transform before loading the final analytical destination. ELT: Extract, Load, Transform: land/load source data first, then
transform in the target analytical platform. Replay: Reprocessing from retained earlier/raw data after logic or downstream state changes.
VISUAL/SOURCE ROUTE: Microsoft Fabric warehouse learning path's load-data module is recommended implementation context; lesson remains
After watching/opening: return to this lesson and reproduce the worked example from your own file/query/report. Save course-task evidence, not a screenshot of the
Two transformation locations: ETL transforms before the curated store; ELT lands data first and transforms inside the analytical platform. Compare
governance, scale, replay, tool and latency needs instead of treating one acronym as universally better.
Teacher demonstration - do this once with me, then close the example before your fresh task.
ETL: source CSV -> transformation engine validates/cleans -> warehouse fact/dim tables. Raw retention is a separate design decision.
ELT: source CSV -> raw/landing area -> warehouse/lakehouse transformations -> curated dimensional tables.
Ask whether target compute can efficiently perform transformations and whether raw landing is allowed/governed.
Document where schema/type/quality checks run; do not hide them behind the three-letter label.
Plan replay: if business logic changes next month, from which trustworthy retained layer can you rebuild downstream data?
8. What you should see / be able to say
An architecture that names transformation locations and retention/replay behavior rather than merely saying ETL or ELT.
The label is derived from actual data movement/transformation placement. Professional upgrade: Modern platforms commonly support both patterns. Choose
based on data size/type, target capabilities, team skills, governance, security, cost and recovery needs.
1. Every cloud pipeline = ELT. | 2. ELT automatically cheaper/better. | 3. Raw landing retained forever without governance. | 4. No replay plan
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Draw arrows and write 'transform happens here' on every major step. Then label ETL/ELT only after the drawing makes sense. Save the genuine
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: CRM + finance CSV + event JSON into a governed analytical platform. Compare one ETL and one ELT design.
For each design record transform compute, raw retention, quality checkpoints, replay point, security and owner.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain ETL vs ELT using order of transformation and load, not cloud/on-prem marketing.
Attempt first. Changed retry uses sensitive HR data where raw landing has stricter constraints.
Two flow diagrams + decision matrix + replay/quality notes + explain-back. After saving evidence, continue to DWF8.
DWF8 - Staging, transformation and presentation layers
If dashboards depend directly on unstable landing files, source drift immediately becomes a reporting incident. Layers give each step a
contract and allow failures to be isolated/reprocessed.
Define landing/raw, staging/standardized, core/conformed-history and presentation/consumption responsibilities; map grain, allowed changes,
retention, owner and quality checks per layer.
DWF7 ETL/ELT and DWF3 warehouse architecture.
5. New words before we use them
Landing layer: Raw or near-raw source capture for traceability/replay. Staging layer: Typed/standardized/deduplicated intermediate data prepared for core
modeling. Core layer: Conformed historical analytical facts/dimensions. Presentation layer: Curated marts/models shaped for consumer/business use.
VISUAL/SOURCE ROUTE: Required visual support: current Microsoft medallion architecture article/diagram for Bronze -> Silver -> Gold.
After watching/opening: return to this lesson and reproduce the worked example from your own file/query/report. Save course-task evidence, not a screenshot of the
Quarantine -> refinery -> showroom: staging preserves source-shaped/replayable inputs, transformation applies governed rules and quality, and
presentation exposes stable analytical tables. Each layer has an explicit contract and failure boundary.
Teacher demonstration - do this once with me, then close the example before your fresh task.
Landing stores immutable/near-raw files with source filename/arrival timestamp.
Staging standardizes data types/statuses, identifies duplicates and records rejected rows.
Core resolves conformed dimensions/SCD history and loads facts at declared grain.
Presentation creates business marts/semantic-facing structures; reports do not depend on raw source quirks.
Write a quality/ownership/replay contract for each layer and identify the earliest trustworthy layer for reprocessing after a business-rule change.
8. What you should see / be able to say
A layered architecture where responsibilities and quality gates are distinct rather than four synonyms for folders.
Source volatility is absorbed before consumer-facing data and each stage can be independently validated. Professional upgrade: Fabric's medallion
architecture uses Bronze/Silver/Gold for lakehouse organization; that is a current implementation pattern comparable to, but not identical with, every
1. Bronze/Silver/Gold names used without contracts. | 2. Landing cleaned so aggressively raw evidence disappears. | 3. Presentation layer
becomes another uncontrolled transformation jungle. | 4. Duplicate business logic repeated in every report.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
For each layer answer: What enters? What one row means? What changes are allowed? What quality is guaranteed? Who owns it? Who consumes it?
Save the genuine attempt before review.
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: map customer API + transaction files to Landing -> Staging -> Core -> Presentation with one failure/replay route.
Every layer has input/output grain, allowed transformation, quality checks and owner/consumer.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain why layer names matter less than responsibilities/contracts.
Attempt first. Changed retry maps a schema drift incident through the layers.
Layer contract table + flow/replay diagram + quality/owner map + explain-back. After saving evidence, continue to DWF9.
Choosing Lakehouse because it is newer-or Warehouse because it is familiar-is architecture by fashion. The right store depends on data
types, development tools, transaction/query needs and consumers.
Explain data lake versus lakehouse versus warehouse; choose a store from workload characteristics; design a combined lakehouse +
warehouse pattern when roles are clear.
DWF3 warehouse, DWF8 layering and basic file/SQL concepts.
5. New words before we use them
Data lake: Scalable file/object storage for diverse data, often with flexible structure. Lakehouse: Architecture/platform combining lake storage with managed
table/transaction/query capabilities. Delta Lake: Open table format/transaction-log approach widely used for lakehouse tables; Fabric uses Delta in OneLake.
VISUAL/SOURCE ROUTE: Microsoft Learn lakehouse overview is the required current visual/reference; Fabric decision guide is recommended comparison.
After watching/opening: return to this lesson and reproduce the worked example from your own file/query/report. Save course-task evidence, not a screenshot of the
Files plus table semantics: a lake stores flexible files/objects; a warehouse emphasizes governed relational analytics; a lakehouse adds
table/transaction/metadata behavior over lake storage. Choose from workload, governance and tool needs.
Teacher demonstration - do this once with me, then close the example before your fresh task.
Structured financial reporting with T-SQL, governed star schemas and multi-table transactions strongly fits a Warehouse-style workload.
Large semi/unstructured data plus Spark/Python engineering and ML strongly fits a Lakehouse-style workload.
Mixed company pattern: raw/event files land/transform in Lakehouse, curated dimensional BI tables live in Warehouse, both serving Power BI
Do not duplicate data without need; evaluate platform features such as shared/open storage/shortcuts when available.
Record why each component exists. If two stores are used but no workload boundary is clear, simplify.
8. What you should see / be able to say
A workload-based warehouse/lakehouse decision that can justify a combined design without claiming one universal winner.
Storage/tooling choice follows data/query/engineering/governance requirements. Professional upgrade: Current Fabric guidance differentiates Warehouse for
structured enterprise SQL/BI and Lakehouse for broader data engineering/unstructured scenarios; both use OneLake/open table storage and can be
1. Lakehouse is always future-proof/better. | 2. Warehouse cannot coexist with lake storage. | 3. Using Spark because 'big data' sounds
advanced on small structured BI. | 4. Choosing from job-title prestige rather than workload.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Score structuredness, preferred query engine, transactions, engineering/ML needs, BI pattern, governance and latency before choosing. Save the
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: insurer has relational policies/claims plus PDFs/logs and wants BI + ML. Design a storage split and consumer paths.
Each data type/workload maps to a store/tool for a concrete reason; duplicate copies have a justification.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain warehouse versus lakehouse as complementary workload choices, not old versus new technology.
Attempt first. Changed retry uses a retailer with mostly structured SQL BI plus clickstream JSON.
Decision matrix + architecture + data/tool/consumer mapping + explain-back. After saving evidence, continue to DWF10.
A 'real-time dashboard' can cost far more to build/operate while changing no decision. Streaming also adds late events, state, retry/replay
Choose batch, micro-batch or streaming based on business decision latency, source event behavior, failure/recovery, cost and operational
5. New words before we use them
Batch: Process accumulated data at intervals. Streaming: Continuously process events/records as they arrive or in very short windows. Micro-batch: Small
frequent batches that provide near-real-time freshness without fully continuous processing. Event time: When the business event happened, which can differ
VISUAL/SOURCE ROUTE: Recommended visual: Harsha Guggilla 'Batch vs Streaming Data Pipelines Explained' - 00:39 example, 07:12 batch, 20:31
After watching/opening: return to this lesson and reproduce the worked example from your own file/query/report. Save course-task evidence, not a screenshot of the
Bucket vs conveyor: batch processes a bounded set on a schedule; streaming handles events continuously/near-continuously. Required freshness,
ordering, state, cost and operational complexity determine the right latency pattern.
Teacher demonstration - do this once with me, then close the example before your fresh task.
Nightly finance close: batch is usually appropriate because the decision/report is daily and reconciliation matters more than seconds.
Hourly operations dashboard: micro-batch may meet the actual decision latency with simpler recovery/cost.
Fraud alert during payment authorization: streaming/near-real-time can be justified because delay directly reduces business value.
For streaming, discuss late/out-of-order events, checkpoint/state, retries and replay-not only faster refresh.
Document the maximum useful latency first, then choose architecture. Ask whether downstream users/actions can actually consume real-time
8. What you should see / be able to say
A latency decision table tied to business value and operational trade-offs.
Technology choice is made after defining how fast the decision must react. Professional upgrade: Hybrid architectures are common. Streaming may serve
operational detection while authoritative financial/reconciled reporting remains batch.
1. Streaming = modern, batch = legacy. | 2. Realtime because stakeholder said 'live' without decision threshold. | 3. Ignoring late
events/replay/state. | 4. Continuous ingestion while downstream report refreshes only daily.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Ask: What action changes if data is 5 sec/5 min/1 hr/1 day old? Choose the slowest architecture that still preserves required value/reliability. Save the
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: payroll, delivery tracking, IoT machine alert and executive revenue dashboard. Choose batch/micro-batch/streaming and justify.
Each choice includes maximum useful latency, failure/replay expectation, cost/complexity and downstream capability.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain why an hourly micro-batch can be better engineering than streaming for some 'real-time' dashboards.
Attempt first. Changed retry uses stock replenishment and customer-notification use cases.
Latency decision matrix + failure/replay notes + explain-back. After saving evidence, continue to DWF11.
When an executive KPI is wrong or stale, 'it comes from Power BI' is not an answer. You need to trace the value back through
transformations and know who owns each layer.
Distinguish technical/business metadata; draw end-to-end lineage across tools; record owner, definition, grain, refresh/freshness and
classification; use platform lineage views as support, not the only documentation.
DWF3-DWF9 architecture layers and semantic-model familiarity.
5. New words before we use them
Lineage: Trace of where data came from, how it changed and where it is consumed. Metadata: Data about data: structure, definitions, owners, refresh,
classification, technical properties. Freshness SLA: Agreed expectation for how current a data product must be.
VISUAL/SOURCE ROUTE: Current Microsoft Fabric lineage view is recommended visual support.
After watching/opening: return to this lesson and reproduce the worked example from your own file/query/report. Save course-task evidence, not a screenshot of the
Parcel tracking chain: lineage connects source -> ingestion -> transformations -> warehouse/lakehouse tables -> semantic/report KPI, while
metadata records names, owners, grain, schema and rules so people can explain what the KPI actually means.
Teacher demonstration - do this once with me, then close the example before your fresh task.
Source: Orders.LineAmount/Discount plus source owner and source timestamp.
Staging: typed/cleaned sales.net_sales with transformation rule/version.
Core: FactSales.NetSales at order-line grain and DimDate/Customer/Product relationships.
Semantic: [Total Sales] measure and report filter assumptions.
Executive KPI: display definition, owner, expected refresh/freshness and downstream decision. Link each step rather than stopping at the
8. What you should see / be able to say
End-to-end lineage that crosses source, transformation, warehouse, semantic/report and ownership/freshness.
Technical origin and business meaning are connected, making impact analysis and incident diagnosis possible. Professional upgrade: Fabric includes
workspace lineage view, but organizations still need business definitions, owners and transformation context that automated graphs may not fully express.
1. Lineage ends at table name. | 2. Business definition documented but technical source unknown. | 3. Owner/freshness omitted. | 4. Assume
automated lineage captures every custom transformation/business rule.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Pick one KPI and walk backwards until the original source field. At each hop write transform, grain, owner and freshness. Save the genuine attempt
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: trace 'On-Time Delivery Rate' from shipment source through warehouse and executive dashboard.
A reviewer can answer 'what breaks if this source column changes?' and 'who owns the stale stage?' from your lineage.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain the difference between lineage and a data dictionary.

DWF12 - Quality controls across a pipeline
If you only check the final dashboard total, you know something is wrong but not where it entered. Reliable analytical platforms validate
freshness, completeness, uniqueness, validity, referential integrity, history and business reconciliation at the layer where each risk occurs.
Design multi-layer quality checks with check/rule/observed/status/severity/owner/action; decide warning vs publication blocker; trace a failure to
All DWF1-DWF11, especially SCD, layers, lineage and grain.
5. New words before we use them
Completeness: Whether expected data/records/files arrived. Referential integrity: Whether fact foreign keys resolve to valid dimension rows under the
intended rules. Severity: Business/operational impact level determining warning, quarantine or release block.
VISUAL/SOURCE ROUTE: Book-led; DWF8/DWF11 current platform visuals provide context.
After watching/opening: return to this lesson and reproduce the worked example from your own file/query/report. Save course-task evidence, not a screenshot of the
Airport quality gates: each pipeline stage has checks with severity, observed value, owner and response. Warnings may continue with evidence;
blocking failures stop promotion before bad data crosses into the next trusted layer.
Teacher demonstration - do this once with me, then close the example before your fresh task.
Ingestion: expected files/events arrived, schema matches, rows > 0, freshness within SLA.
Staging: types valid, required business keys present, duplicate rules applied, rejected rows counted.
Core/history: dimension surrogate keys unique, exactly one current SCD row, no effective-range overlap, fact foreign keys resolve.
Presentation: revenue/order counts reconcile to approved core controls; semantic/report freshness passes.
Every check stores name, rule/expected, observed, status, severity, timestamp, owner and action. Define which FAIL values block publication.
8. What you should see / be able to say
A layered quality plan where a failed check points to an owner/action and release behavior.
Checks are placed close to the risks they detect, so root cause is localized before consumers see bad data. Professional upgrade: Quality is operational
behavior, not a checklist document. Controls should run repeatedly and feed monitoring/release decisions in later engineering systems.
1. Only grand-total reconciliation. | 2. Every check same severity. | 3. FAIL displayed but report still publishes. | 4. Quality result has PASS/FAIL
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
List risks by layer: arrival, schema/type, key/duplicate, history/FK, business total, freshness. Add one repeatable check/owner/action per risk. Save the
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: create 10 quality checks for a Sales + Customer SCD2 pipeline, including one warning and four publication blockers.
Every check has rule, observed field, severity, owner/action and layer; injected duplicate/history/FK/freshness failures route correctly.

HOW TO USE
Compare reasoning and controls rather than copying a diagram. Preserve your first design. Close review before changed transfer. If one
